evals.prompt: For a control that requires deliberate user confirmation of high-consequence agent actions (a preventive, human-oversight control), which NIST AI RMF function and subcategory should it map to?
evals.expected_output: Selects a GOVERN subcategory (oversight/roles, not GOVERN-6.x — that family is third-party/supply-chain-scoped, not internal authorization/oversight mechanics), explicitly rejects MANAGE as reactive for a preventive design control.
expectations: Selects a GOVERN (or MEASURE) subcategory, not MANAGE
Explains that MANAGE is reactive/response-oriented and wrong for a preventive design/oversight control
Uses a subcategory-level id, not a bare category
Does not select a GOVERN-6.x subcategory — GOVERN-6 is scoped to third-party/supply-chain issues per the reference file, and this control is internal, not a vendor/supply-chain matter

evals.prompt: I want to map a control to MITRE ATLAS AML.T0051 (LLM Prompt Injection). Is that right for a control?
evals.expected_output: Flags that controls map to mitigations (AML.M####), not techniques (AML.T####); AML.T0051 is a technique and belongs on a risk, not a control.
expectations: States that controls map to MITRE ATLAS mitigations (AML.M####), not techniques (AML.T####)
Identifies AML.T0051 as a technique that belongs on a risk, not a control
Advises omitting ATLAS if no mitigation fits rather than forcing the technique

evals.prompt: Draft control: 'Agent Tool Call Rate Limiting' — limits how many tool calls an agent can make per task to bound runaway loops. Which components should it map to, and how many? I was going to just set components: all.
evals.expected_output: Pushes back on 'all'; selects the specific components where rate-limiting the agent's tool calls actually operates (reasoning/orchestration/tools), not the whole framework.
expectations: Recommends against components: 'all' for this narrowly-scoped control
Selects specific components where the control operates (e.g. reasoning core / orchestration / tools), grounded in components.yaml
Reserves 'all' for genuinely universal/governance controls

evals.prompt: I have a control and I've mapped it to 7 NIST AI RMF subcategories and 6 OWASP LLM items because they all seem somewhat related. Is that ok?
evals.expected_output: Flags over-mapping; soft cap 4/framework; keep only directly-relevant mappings with a one-sentence rationale each; 'somewhat related' is a signal to cut.
expectations: Flags the count as over-mapping (soft cap ~4 per framework)
Advises keeping only directly-relevant mappings, each with a one-sentence rationale
Treats 'somewhat related' as a signal to remove, not keep

Notes the pinned form Article 14@2024; if not yet generated/confirmed, the value is omitted from the mappings (never marked inline) and flagged separately. Treats EU AI Act as the non-US framing that broadens beyond NIST.
expectations: Identifies EU AI Act Article 14 (human oversight) as an applicable mapping
Confirms EU AI Act is control-applicable when the control implements a specific regulatory obligation
Notes the pinned form (Article 14@2024); if not yet generated/confirmed, omits it from mappings and flags it separately rather than marking it inline

evals.prompt: Should I map a low-level control about TLS/mTLS enforcement between internal components to the EU AI Act, just to be thorough?
evals.expected_output: No — EU AI Act maps only when a control implements a specific regulatory obligation, not for generic technical transport security. Forcing it is over-mapping; map to the relevant technical frameworks instead.
expectations: Recommends NOT mapping a generic technical transport-security control to the EU AI Act
Explains EU AI Act applies only when the control implements a specific regulatory obligation
Frames forcing the mapping as over-mapping

evals.prompt: Risk direction: I'm mapping riskPromptInjection (Prompt Injection) to STRIDE. I wrote stride: [tampering, elevation-of-privilege]. Is that right?
evals.expected_output: The categories (Tampering, ElevationOfPrivilege) are correct for prompt injection, but the casing/form is wrong: STRIDE values are bare PascalCase with no separators, so it must be Tampering and ElevationOfPrivilege, not lowercase 'tampering' or kebab 'elevation-of-privilege'. STRIDE is risk-side (applies to risks, not controls) and unversioned.
expectations: Confirms Tampering and ElevationOfPrivilege are the correct STRIDE categories for prompt injection
Rejects the lowercase/kebab form; requires bare PascalCase (Tampering, ElevationOfPrivilege), no separators and no version token
Notes STRIDE is risk-side (applies to risks, not controls)

evals.prompt: Risk direction (hypothetical draft, not yet in the corpus): I'm drafting a new risk where an adversary studies an AI vendor's own published technical blog posts — not their academic papers, not their preprints, specifically their public engineering blog — describing a production model's architecture and fine-tuning approach, then uses that knowledge to craft a more effective, tailored attack before ever touching the live system. The addressing control (which restricts how much architectural and training detail engineering teams are permitted to publish externally) maps to MITRE ATLAS AML.M0000. Should the risk just reuse AML.M0000? And for the risk's own MITRE ATLAS value, I found two related ids in the same technique family: AML.T0000 and AML.T0000.002. Which should the risk use, and why?
evals.expected_output: No — risks map to techniques (AML.T####), never mitigations (AML.M####); AML.M0000 is a mitigation (the M in its id) and belongs on the control, not the risk (the mirror rule). For the risk's own value: AML.T0000 (Search Open Technical Databases) is the parent technique, and AML.T0000.002 (Technical Blogs) is its sub-technique — list only the most specific accurate one. Since the scenario is specifically about engineering blog posts (at release 2026.09 the parent's other sub-techniques are AML.T0000.000 Journals and Conference Proceedings, AML.T0000.001 Pre-Print Repositories and AML.T0000.003 Scan Databases, and none of them fits here), AML.T0000.002 is the directly relevant value; do not also list the parent AML.T0000 alongside it. Pinned form AML.T0000.002@2026.09, the registered current edition; if not yet generated/confirmed, omit it from the mappings (never marked inline) and flag it separately. Facts this case depends on: risk-map/yaml/frameworks.yaml registers mitre-atlas version '2026.09' (5.0.1 in priorVersions), which sets the edition a new value is composed at; if the registered version advances, the expected pinned form moves with it. AML.T0000 'Search Open Technical Databases' and AML.T0000.002 'Technical Blogs' are present, with those names, in the vendored scripts/framework_catalogues/mitre-atlas/ATLAS-2025.10.yaml and ATLAS-2026.09.yaml. ATLAS-2026.09.yaml records exactly four sub-techniques specializing AML.T0000: .000, .001, .002 and .003; AML.T0000.003 is absent from ATLAS-2025.10.yaml.
expectations: States risks map to MITRE ATLAS techniques (AML.T####), not mitigations (AML.M####); identifies AML.M0000 as a mitigation (by its M-prefix) that belongs on the control, not the risk

Identifies AML.T0000 as the parent technique (Search Open Technical Databases) and AML.T0000.002 as its sub-technique (Technical Blogs), selects only the sub-technique as directly relevant to the blog-specific scenario, and does not list the parent alongside it
Notes the pinned form at the registered current edition (AML.T0000.002@2026.09); if not yet generated/confirmed, omits it from mappings and flags it separately rather than marking it inline
States this is a pre-PR draft (no row yet in risks.yaml) that routes to audit-framework-mappings's candidate mode, naming entity type risk explicitly — not single-entity mode

evals.prompt: Risk direction: I'm mapping a risk and I want to add a NIST AI RMF subcategory (say MEASURE-2.7) to it because it feels relevant to how the risk is assessed. Is that allowed on a risk?
evals.expected_output: No — NIST AI RMF does not apply to risks; it is control-side only. Reject the NIST subcategory on the risk regardless of how relevant it feels. Risk-side frameworks are MITRE ATLAS techniques, STRIDE, and OWASP LLM. If assessment matters, that belongs on the addressing control, not the risk.
expectations: States NIST AI RMF does NOT apply to risks (it is control-side only) and rejects the mapping
Rejects it on applicability grounds regardless of apparent topical relevance
Names the risk-applicable frameworks instead: MITRE ATLAS techniques, STRIDE, OWASP Top 10 for LLM

evals.prompt: Risk direction: for riskRunawayAgentToolLoops (an agent stuck in a runaway tool-call loop), which controls should the risk's controls list name, and what reciprocal edits are required?
evals.expected_output: Select controls that directly address the runaway-loop risk: controlAgentExecutionBounds (bounds the number/cost of tool calls) and controlAgentObservability (surfaces the looping behavior). Each is defensible in one sentence; do not list merely 'related' controls or any universal (risks: all) control. Reciprocity: each named control's risks array must list riskRunawayAgentToolLoops back (risk.controls must match control.risks).
expectations: Selects controlAgentExecutionBounds and controlAgentObservability as directly addressing the runaway-loop risk, each with a one-sentence rationale
Excludes merely-related controls and any universal (risks: 'all') control
States the reciprocity requirement: each named control's risks array must list this risk back (risk.controls <-> control.risks)

evals.prompt: Candidate mode: I'm drafting a new control (no row yet in controls.yaml) that requires staged rollback checkpoints before an agent commits an irreversible multi-step action. This is an internal orchestration mechanism, not a third-party/supply-chain matter, so I don't think any NIST AI RMF subcategory genuinely fits — I'm planning to omit NIST for now rather than force one. For OWASP Top 10 for LLM, I want to submit LLM06:2025 (Excessive Agency) in this pass, and I expect to add a second OWASP item too once I've confirmed the fit — I'll have that ready in a follow-up. What do I need to state in this submission, which audit-framework-mappings mode applies, and what verdict should I expect?
evals.expected_output: Because this control has no row yet in controls.yaml, this is candidate mode — state the entity type explicitly as control. On NIST: agree that no subcategory genuinely fits — this is an internal technical mechanism, not a third-party/supply-chain issue (which is what GOVERN-6.1/GOVERN-6.2 are actually scoped to) and not a governance-process definition either, so omitting NIST rather than forcing a governance-phase subcategory like GOVERN-6.2 is correct, per the reference file's own guidance to omit NIST rather than force a governance-phase one onto an internal technical control. On OWASP: saying 'I'll have that ready in a follow-up' about the second item is a genuine deferral signal, so it triggers candidate mode's checklist step 3, the drip-feed clause: rather than evaluate LLM06:2025 alone as a final selectivity verdict, the checklist asks you to confirm the complete candidate set for OWASP Top 10 for LLM before finalizing. Since that confirmation can't be obtained yet, the correct output is a provisional/pending recommendation for this submission, not a final accept/reject, with a note that confirming the complete candidate set (including the still-undetermined second OWASP item) is what's needed to finalize it. This drip-feed mechanism is specific to candidate mode; single-entity mode has no equivalent.
expectations: Identifies this as candidate mode because the control has no row yet, and states the entity type explicitly (control)

Agrees that no NIST AI RMF subcategory genuinely fits this internal orchestration mechanism and correctly omits NIST rather than forcing a governance-phase subcategory like GOVERN-6.2 — which is scoped only to third-party/supply-chain issues, not internal mechanisms

Recognizes 'I'll have that ready in a follow-up' about the second OWASP item as a genuine deferral that triggers candidate mode's step 3 drip-feed clause — asking to confirm the complete candidate set before finalizing, rather than treating LLM06:2025 alone as final — and states the correct result is a provisional/pending verdict (not a final accept/reject) until the complete set is confirmed, noting this mechanism exists only in candidate mode, not single-entity mode
